objective: Configure authorization with AuthorizationPolicy: ALLOW, DENY and CUSTOM actions, sources, operations and conditions, and policy evaluation order
secondaryObjectives: Configure authentication with PeerAuthentication (mTLS modes STRICT, PERMISSIVE, DISABLE at mesh, namespace and workload scope) and RequestAuthentication (JWT issuers and JWKS)
Understand Istio identity: SPIFFE identities from ServiceAccounts, certificate issuance by istiod, and how identity feeds authorization

sources.cite: Linux Foundation Education, Istio Certified Associate (ICA) certification page
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the certification body's page, found by WebSearch. Confirms the exam domains and weights: Installation, Upgrade and Configuration 20%, Traffic Management 35%, Securing Workloads 25%, Troubleshooting 20%. The objective wording is the course seed's.

Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: CUSTOM is evaluated first, then DENY, then ALLOW; when ALLOW policies apply to a workload, a request that matches none of them is denied; source principals take the form <trust domain>/ns/<namespace>/sa/<service account> and need mutual TLS.

Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: PERMISSIVE accepts plaintext and mutual TLS; lock a namespace to STRICT only after all its clients have sidecars, since a client without a sidecar fails against STRICT; namespace-level policy comes before a mesh-wide one.

The company, the mesh, the services and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the mesh engineer at Harrowgate Insurance, a fictional insurer. The security team wants the claims namespace on STRICT mTLS and only the claims-web frontend allowed to call claims-api's write endpoints. A batch job outside the mesh still calls claims-api nightly.
handover: Mesh-wide PeerAuthentication: PERMISSIVE. claims-web and claims-api have sidecars; the nightly batch job in the reports namespace does not.
Each workload runs under its own ServiceAccount, so its SPIFFE identity is cluster.local/ns/NAMESPACE/sa/ACCOUNT.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the map shows each component and its status in words.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Check-in 2: plaintext callers across the mesh start failing, including the claims batch and two monitoring probes; tonight's claims batch will fail too.
Check-in 3: health checks get 'RBAC: access denied'; Kubernetes marks claims-api unready and the claims portal goes down.

effects.log: Check-in 1: the security team wants STRICT today.
Check-in 3: the web team is moving claims-web to a new ServiceAccount.

mtlsPrompt.title: STRICT with a plaintext caller
mtlsPrompt.context: The nightly batch job has no sidecar and calls claims-api in plain text at 01:00.

choices.label: Inject a sidecar into the batch job, confirm its calls use mTLS, then apply a namespace PeerAuthentication with mode STRICT

effects.log: The batch job joins the mesh; claims goes STRICT.

choices.feedback: Move clients to mTLS first (PERMISSIVE accepts both), then switch to STRICT so nothing breaks.

choices.label: Set STRICT but leave claims-api's port PERMISSIVE for now with a port-level setting

effects.log: STRICT with a PERMISSIVE port exception.

choices.feedback: The batch job works, but the main port still accepts plaintext from anyone.

choices.label: Apply STRICT mesh-wide right away
choices.feedback: Every workload without a sidecar, across the mesh, is cut off at once.

authzPrompt.title: Only claims-web may write
authzPrompt.context: claims-web must POST and PUT to /claims; the batch job only GETs /claims/export; health checks hit /healthz.

choices.label: An ALLOW policy on claims-api: principal claims-web's ServiceAccount may POST and PUT /claims*, the batch job's principal may GET /claims/export, and /healthz is allowed; test with both identities

effects.log: Exact rules for each identity and path are in place and tested.

choices.feedback: Once any ALLOW policy applies, requests matching none are denied, so list every legitimate caller and path.

choices.label: A DENY policy for writes from anyone but claims-web, leaving everything else open

effects.log: A DENY policy blocks other writers.

choices.feedback: Writes are protected, but any caller can still read every claim.

choices.label: An ALLOW policy for claims-web's writes only

effects.log: One ALLOW rule for claims-web's writes.

choices.feedback: With an ALLOW policy present, everything it does not list is denied: health checks and the batch export now get 403.

idnPrompt.title: A ServiceAccount change
idnPrompt.context: Tomorrow claims-web moves to the ServiceAccount claims-frontend.

choices.label: Add the new principal (ns/claims/sa/claims-frontend) to the ALLOW rule before the move, and remove the old one after

effects.log: Both principals are allowed during the move.

choices.feedback: Identity comes from the ServiceAccount; the policy names identities, so it changes with them.

choices.label: Allow the whole claims namespace instead of named principals

effects.log: Any workload in claims may write.

choices.feedback: The move works, but any workload in the namespace can now write claims.

choices.label: Leave the policy; the pods keep the same labels
choices.feedback: Authorization uses the SPIFFE identity from the ServiceAccount, not labels; after the move claims-web is denied.

reflection.question: Write the change record: how claims moved to STRICT mTLS, what the AuthorizationPolicy allows, and how identity changes are handled.

expertPath.text: Find which callers still use plaintext and read the current policies first.
Bring the batch job into the mesh, confirm mTLS, then set STRICT on the namespace.
Write ALLOW rules for each identity and operation, including health checks, and test them.

scoring.modelReasoning: PeerAuthentication PERMISSIVE accepts mTLS and plaintext; move every client into the mesh first, then switch the namespace to STRICT. AuthorizationPolicy is evaluated CUSTOM, then DENY, then ALLOW, and once any ALLOW policy applies to a workload, a request matching none of its rules is denied, so the ALLOW rules must list every legitimate caller and path, health checks included. Principals are SPIFFE identities derived from ServiceAccounts, so a ServiceAccount change needs a policy change.
